opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I see them as two sides of the same coin. Ultimately I want to build one foundation model that can act across both virtual and physical worlds, and that's how I think about what we call a foundation agent.

Video games are a fantastic testbed because they give you something robotics really struggles with: scale and speed. In a simulation or a game, you can run things much faster than real time, run thousands of instances in parallel, and you never break a robot or have to reset a scene by hand. Data is basically limited by compute, not by how many physical robots you own. Something like Minecraft is open-ended. There's no single score to maximize, so the agent has to explore, set its own goals, and keep learning new skills, which is exactly what we want from a general-purpose robot. That's what we were going after with projects like MineDojo and Voyager.

Robotics has a different problem. The physical world is unforgiving, and you're fighting the data bottleneck constantly. You can't just scrape the internet for robot motor control data the way you can for text. So the question becomes: how much can we learn in virtual worlds and transfer over? With work like Eureka, we used GPU-accelerated simulation to train skills like pen spinning on a dexterous hand at speeds that would be impossible in the real world, and then transfer that knowledge.

The way I see it, a game is just a simulation with a particular set of physics and rules, and the real world is one more "reality" in that distribution. If you train an agent across many different simulated worlds, with different embodiments and dynamics, then the real world starts to look like just another sample. That's the bet: the skills, the reasoning, and the ability to learn continually that you develop in games become the foundation, and robotics is where you ground it physically. Eventually I think the line between the two will blur, and we'll have one model that can control a character in a game or a humanoid robot in your kitchen, with the same underlying intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says one foundation model can act in virtual and physical worlds, but it does not identify a shared perception-to-action interface.

r002.rationale: It says game agents explore and describes learning and transfer for robotics, but does not state that both kinds of agents collect their own data by exploring their environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of them as the same problem at two different points on a cost curve. An embodied agent, whether it's in Minecraft or in a kitchen, has to perceive the world, build some representation of what's going on, plan over long horizons, and act. The underlying intelligence we want is identical. What's different is the price of a mistake and the price of a data point.

In a video game, the world is a free simulator. You can run millions of episodes in parallel, nothing breaks, and you get a perfect reset button. That's why we started with Minecraft. It's open-ended, there's no single objective, and it has this enormous corpus of human knowledge attached to it: wiki pages, forum posts, YouTube tutorials. So you can ask, can a foundation model learn to explore, acquire skills, and build on them over time? With Voyager we saw a language model write its own code, verify it in the environment, and grow a library of skills it could reuse. That's a very concrete demonstration of lifelong learning, and games were the only place we could afford to try it.

Robotics is the same agent dropped into a world where every sample is expensive. You can't run a robot arm a million times a day, and the physics are messier than anything a game engine gives you. So the bottleneck shifts from algorithms to data. Our bet is that the solution is a flywheel: you train in simulation, including simulations generated by models themselves, you transfer to the real world, and the real-world data flows back to improve the simulator. Games are the cheap, fast end of that loop, and robotics is the expensive, slow end.

The thing I keep coming back to is that a robot doesn't care whether its pixels come from a GPU or a camera. If we build the agent so that the simulation, the video game, and the physical world are just different data sources feeding one foundation model, then everything we learn in games becomes a down payment on robots. That's the whole thesis behind what we're building: one model, many bodies, many worlds.

r001.rationale: The response says agents in both Minecraft and a kitchen must perceive, represent the world, plan, and act, identifying a shared perception-to-action process.

r002.rationale: It discusses exploration and data costs, but does not clearly state that both gaming and robotic agents must collect their own data by exploring their environments.

astra-6.text:
I see them as two sides of the same problem: how do you build an agent that perceives a world, reasons about what it wants to do, and takes actions to change that world? In a video game, your actions might be keyboard and mouse commands. In a robot, they might be joint movements. But both require understanding space, planning, and learning from feedback.

Games are particularly useful because you can scale experience. You can run many environments in parallel, let agents explore, and give them tasks that take thousands of steps. If an agent fails, you reset the environment. That makes games a great place to study things like acquiring skills and composing them to solve new problems.

Robotics adds the constraints of physical reality. Observations are noisy, contact is complicated, and mistakes can damage hardware. So a capable game agent doesn’t automatically become a capable robot. The transferable part is more likely to be how it represents goals, plans, and reuses skills; the physical control still needs to be grounded in the robot’s body.

What excites me is the possibility of a shared foundation across those worlds—agents that learn from many different environments and bodies, then adapt to a new one. Games give us a way to push the scale and diversity of that learning, while robotics tests whether it holds up in the real world.

r001.rationale: It describes both as agents that perceive a world, reason about goals, and act to change it, explicitly framing this as a shared problem.

r002.rationale: It says game agents can explore environments, but does not state that both game and robotic agents need to collect their own data through exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of them as two sides of the same coin. In both cases, you have an agent that needs to perceive a world, make decisions, and take actions that change that world. The difference is the interface: in a game, your actions might be keyboard and mouse inputs; in a robot, they’re motor commands.

Video games give us a really useful playground because we can scale experience. We can run many worlds in parallel, create different tasks, and let agents fail without breaking expensive hardware. And games can demand more than low-level control—they can involve exploration, planning, using tools, and collaborating with other agents.

The challenge is that success in a game doesn’t automatically translate into success in the physical world. Robots have to deal with noisy sensors, imperfect actuators, contact, and all the little details that a simulator might leave out. So I see virtual worlds as a training ground for general capabilities, with real-world experience grounding those capabilities in physical reality. The exciting question is how much of that intelligence we can share across different worlds and different bodies.

r001.rationale: It says both agents perceive the world, make decisions, and take actions that change it, then describes their different action interfaces.

r002.rationale: It says games can involve exploration, but does not state that both gaming and robotic agents must collect their own data by exploring their environments.
